units.title: What Makes AI Intelligent?
learn_paragraphs:
Intelligence is the ability to learn, reason and solve problems. Humans have it, and
we try to build some of it into machines.
Today's AI is narrow AI: it is good at one task, like recognising faces or translating
text. It cannot do everything a human can.
AI has three main domains: Data Science (numbers and tables), Computer Vision
(images and video) and Natural Language Processing (text and speech).

units.title: The AI Project Cycle
learn_paragraphs:
Every AI project follows a cycle of five stages, called the AI Project Cycle.
1 Problem Scoping – understand the problem. 2 Data Acquisition – collect data. 3
Data Exploration – study the data with charts. 4 Modelling – build the AI model. 5
Evaluation – test how well it works.
After evaluation we often go back and improve. That is why it is a cycle, not a
straight line.

units.title: Problem Scoping with 4Ws
learn_paragraphs:
A good AI project starts with a clear problem. We use the 4Ws Canvas to
understand it.
Who has the problem? What is the problem? Where does it happen? Why does
solving it matter?
Then we write a problem statement: “Our [who] have a problem that [what]
when/while [where]. An ideal solution would [why].”

units.think_and_talk: Why should we talk to the stakeholders before building a solution?

units.title: Data Acquisition
learn_paragraphs:
Data acquisition means collecting the data an AI needs to learn.
Data can come from surveys, sensors, cameras, websites, open government data
and records like attendance.
Primary data is collected by us. Secondary data is collected by someone else. Data
must be relevant, reliable and collected with permission.

units.title: Exploring Data with Charts
learn_paragraphs:
Raw data is hard to read. Data exploration uses charts to find patterns and
mistakes.
A bar graph compares groups. A line graph shows change over time. A pie chart
shows parts of a whole.
Choosing the right chart makes the story in the data clear.

units.did_you_know: Florence Nightingale used charts in the 1850s to convince leaders to improve hospitals.

units.title: Algorithms and Flowcharts
learn_paragraphs:
An algorithm is a set of steps to solve a problem. A flowchart draws an algorithm
with shapes.
Oval = Start/End. Rectangle = Process. Diamond = Decision (yes/no). Parallelogram
= Input/Output. Arrows show the flow.
Decisions let algorithms choose different paths, just like AI makes choices.

units.title: Pseudocode and Conditions
learn_paragraphs:
Pseudocode is an algorithm written in simple English-like steps, before real code.
Conditions use IF, ELSE and comparisons like >, < and =. Variables store values like
score or age.
These same ideas are used in Scratch, Python and every AI program.

units.did_you_know: The first computer programmer is often said to be Ada Lovelace, who wrote an algorithm in the 1840s.
units.think_and_talk: Why is it helpful to write pseudocode before real code?

units.title: AI Ethics: Privacy and Bias
learn_paragraphs:
AI uses lots of data, often about people. Privacy means people control their personal
data.
Bias happens when data or design favours some people over others, so the AI is
unfair.
Ethical AI is fair, transparent, safe and respects privacy. Builders must think about
who could be harmed.
